claim: SNI triggers an increase in Aif1 gene expression in the DRGs from day 3, reaching a peak between 7 and 10 days after SNI.
source: We found that Aif1 and Csf1r genes expression were up-regulated from day 3, reaching a peak between 7 and 10 days after SNI (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating time course of gene expression.

claim: SNI triggers an increase in Csf1r gene expression in the DRGs from day 3, reaching a peak between 7 and 10 days after SNI.
source: We found that Aif1 and Csf1r genes expression were up-regulated from day 3, reaching a peak between 7 and 10 days after SNI (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating time course of gene expression.

claim: The number of macrophages (Iba1+ cells) increases in the DRGs at 7 days after SNI.
source: Additionally, immunofluorescence analysis revealed an increased number of macrophages (Iba1+ cells) in the DRGs at 7 days after nerve injury (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The number of CD11b+ Ly6G− cells increases in the DRGs at 7 days after SNI.
source: Using flow cytometry, we confirmed an increase in the number of macrophages (CD11b+ Ly6G− cells) in the DRGs at 7 days after SNI (Figure 1E), while no significant changes were observed in the number of neutrophils (CD11b+ Ly6G+ cells).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No significant changes were observed in the number of neutrophils (CD11b+ Ly6G+ cells) in the DRGs at 7 days after SNI.
source: Using flow cytometry, we confirmed an increase in the number of macrophages (CD11b+ Ly6G− cells) in the DRGs at 7 days after SNI (Figure 1E), while no significant changes were observed in the number of neutrophils (CD11b+ Ly6G+ cells).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CX3CR1+ cells predominate in the sensory ganglia compared to CCR2+ cells in naive conditions.
source: In naive conditions, CX3CR1+ cells predominate in the sensory ganglia compared to CCR2+ cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification in Cx3cr1GFP/+/Ccr2RFP/+ reporter mice shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Approximately 97% of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs are Iba1+ and vice-versa.
source: Noteworthy, we found that ~97% of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs are Iba1+ and vice-versa (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that all resident macrophages in the sensory ganglia are CX3CR1+.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence co-localization analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All resident macrophages in the sensory ganglia are CX3CR1+.
source: Noteworthy, we found that ~97% of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs are Iba1+ and vice-versa (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that all resident macrophages in the sensory ganglia are CX3CR1+.
evidence: Inferred from the high degree of co-localization between CX3CR1 and Iba1 markers.

claim: The number of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs increases after SNI.
source: Notably, while the number of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs increased after SNI (Figure 2B), CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes numbers did not change (Figure 2B), indicating that the circulating CCR2+ monocytes did not infiltrate into the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Cx3cr1GFP/+/Ccr2RFP/+ reporter mice shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CCR2+ inflammatory monocyte numbers do not change in the DRGs after SNI.
source: Notably, while the number of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs increased after SNI (Figure 2B), CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes numbers did not change (Figure 2B), indicating that the circulating CCR2+ monocytes did not infiltrate into the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Cx3cr1GFP/+/Ccr2RFP/+ reporter mice shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Circulating CCR2+ monocytes do not infiltrate into the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Notably, while the number of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs increased after SNI (Figure 2B), CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes numbers did not change (Figure 2B), indicating that the circulating CCR2+ monocytes did not infiltrate into the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of increase in CCR2+ cells despite nerve injury.

claim: Significant CCR2+ blood-monocyte infiltration occurs in the DRGs of HSV-1-infected mice.
source: As expected, we observed a significant CCR2+ blood-monocyte infiltration in the DRGs of HSV-1-infected mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in HSV-1 infection model shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of CD11b+ Ly6C+ Ly6G- cells (peripheral monocytes) does not change in the DRGs after SNI compared to naive animals.
source: Corroborating these data, the number of CD11b+ Ly6C+ Ly6G- cells (peripheral monocytes) did not change in the DRGs after SNI compared to naive animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Cx3cr1 gene expression increases in the DRGs after SNI.
source: In addition, we also found an increase in the expression of Cx3cr1 in the DRGs after SNI, and flow cytometry analysis confirmed a significant increase in the number of CD11b+ CX3CR1+ cells when compared to the naive group (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The number of CD11b+ CX3CR1+ cells increases in the DRGs after SNI compared to the naive group.
source: In addition, we also found an increase in the expression of Cx3cr1 in the DRGs after SNI, and flow cytometry analysis confirmed a significant increase in the number of CD11b+ CX3CR1+ cells when compared to the naive group (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The increase of Cx3cr1 gene expression after SNI does not change in Ccr2−/− mice compared to Ccr2-sufficient animals.
source: Additionally, using deficient mice for the chemokine receptor CCR2 (Ccr2−/− mice), we noticed that the increase of Cx3cr1 gene expression after SNI did not change in these mice compared to Ccr2-sufficient animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing Ccr2−/− and Ccr2+/+ mice shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ccr2−/− mice show a similar number of macrophages in the DRGs compared to WT mice in naive condition.
source: Furthermore, flow cytometry (CD11b+ CX3CR1+ cells) and immunofluorescence (Iba1+ cells) analyses showed a similar number of macrophages in the DRGs from Ccr2−/− mice compared to WT mice in a naive condition and increased at the same level after SNI (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: Macrophages in the DRGs from Ccr2−/− mice increase at the same level as WT mice after SNI.
source: Furthermore, flow cytometry (CD11b+ CX3CR1+ cells) and immunofluorescence (Iba1+ cells) analyses showed a similar number of macrophages in the DRGs from Ccr2−/− mice compared to WT mice in a naive condition and increased at the same level after SNI (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: CCR2+ monocyte infiltration is not required to expand CX3CR1+ resident macrophages in the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury.
source: These results suggest that CCR2+ monocyte infiltration is not required to expand CX3CR1+ resident macrophages in the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that macrophage expansion occurs similarly in Ccr2−/− and WT mice.

claim: The number of macrophages (Iba1+ cells) increases in the DRGs of WT mice 7 days after SNI in parabiosis experiments.
source: In agreement with our earlier results, the number of macrophages (Iba1+ cells) increased in the DRGs of WT mice 7 days after SNI. However, the number of GFP+ cells in the DRGs of WT mice remained constant in both naïve and SNI groups (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in parabiotic mice shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The number of GFP+ cells in the DRGs of WT mice remains constant in both naïve and SNI groups in parabiosis experiments.
source: In agreement with our earlier results, the number of macrophages (Iba1+ cells) increased in the DRGs of WT mice 7 days after SNI. However, the number of GFP+ cells in the DRGs of WT mice remained constant in both naïve and SNI groups (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in parabiotic mice shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Substantial numbers of CCR2+ or CX3CR1+ cells from the parabiotic partner are not detected in the DRGs after SNI.
source: Despite the increase of macrophages (Iba1+ cells) in the DRGs after SNI, we could not detect substantial numbers of CCR2+ or CX3CR1+ cells in SNI compared to naive mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Cx3cr1GFP/+/Ccr2RFP/+ parabiotic mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: In naive condition, the number of Ms4a3Cre-tdTomato/Iba1+ cells are relatively low in the DRGs (~17%).
source: We found that, in naive condition, the number of Ms4a3Cre-tdTomato/Iba1+ cells are relatively low in the DRGs (~17%), indicating a small contribution of hematopoietic-derived monocytes to the pool of resident macrophages in the DRGs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Ms4a3Cre fate-mapping mice shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hematopoietic-derived monocytes make a small contribution to the pool of resident macrophages in the DRGs.
source: We found that, in naive condition, the number of Ms4a3Cre-tdTomato/Iba1+ cells are relatively low in the DRGs (~17%), indicating a small contribution of hematopoietic-derived monocytes to the pool of resident macrophages in the DRGs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Inferred from the low percentage of Ms4a3Cre-tdTomato/Iba1+ cells.

claim: The number of monocytes or monocyte-derived cells in the DRGs does not change significantly after SNI.
source: In addition, the number of monocytes or monocyte-derived cells in the DRGs did not change significantly after SNI (Figure 5A and B), further indicating that blood monocytes are not infiltrating the DRGs after SNI.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Ms4a3Cre fate-mapping mice shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Blood monocytes are not infiltrating the DRGs after SNI.
source: In addition, the number of monocytes or monocyte-derived cells in the DRGs did not change significantly after SNI (Figure 5A and B), further indicating that blood monocytes are not infiltrating the DRGs after SNI.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of increase in Ms4a3Cre-tdTomato cells after SNI.

claim: Neutrophils do not infiltrate the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Since the Ms4a3Cre-tdTomato model also allows the tracing of granulocytes (Liu et al., 2019), these data also indicated that neutrophils did not infiltrate the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from Ms4a3Cre-tdTomato fate-mapping data and cited literature.

claim: The increase in the number of macrophages in the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury is likely to result from the expansion/proliferation of CX3CR1+ resident macrophages regardless of peripheral blood CCR2+ monocytes infiltration.
source: Altogether, these findings strongly suggest that the increase in the number of macrophages in the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury is likely to result from the expansion/proliferation of CX3CR1+ resident macrophages regardless of peripheral blood CCR2+ monocytes infiltration.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental approaches including reporter mice, parabiosis, and fate-mapping.

claim: The expansion of CX3CR1+ macrophages in the DRGs is accompanied by an increase in Ki67+ staining in CX3CR1+ macrophages three days after SNI.
source: Corroborating this hypothesis, we found that the expansion of CX3CR1+ macrophages in the DRGs was accompanied by an increase in Ki67+ staining in CX3CR1+ macrophages, three days after SNI indicating a high proliferation profile (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence co-localization of CX3CR1 and Ki67 shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Seven days after SNI, a significant number of cells are still proliferating, but few of them are CX3CR1+ macrophages.
source: Notably, 7 days after injury, a significant number of cells are still proliferating, however, few of them are CX3CR1+ macrophages. This indicates that other cell populations (e.g. satellite glial cells, Schwann cells, or mesenchymal cells) also undergo proliferation after SNI.
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Other cell populations (e.g. satellite glial cells, Schwann cells, or mesenchymal cells) undergo proliferation after SNI.
source: Notably, 7 days after injury, a significant number of cells are still proliferating, however, few of them are CX3CR1+ macrophages. This indicates that other cell populations (e.g. satellite glial cells, Schwann cells, or mesenchymal cells) also undergo proliferation after SNI.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of Ki67+ cells that are not CX3CR1+ at 7 days post-injury.

claim: The increase in the number of Ki67+ macrophages in the DRGs from Ccr2−/− mice after SNI is similar to the numbers observed in the DRGs from WT mice.
source: Noteworthy, the increase in the number of Ki67+ macrophages in the DRGs from Ccr2−/− mice after SNI was similar to the numbers observed in the DRGs from WT mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Ccr2−/− mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Intrathecal treatment of mice with AraC reduces SNI-induced mechanical pain hypersensitivity (mechanical allodynia).
source: In fact, the intrathecal treatment (which targets cells in the DRGs; Wang et al., 2005) of mice with AraC, a cell proliferation inhibitor, reduced SNI-induced mechanical pain hypersensitivity (mechanical allodynia) that was associated with decreased numbers of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing and immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Intrathecal treatment of mice with AraC is associated with decreased numbers of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs.
source: In fact, the intrathecal treatment (which targets cells in the DRGs; Wang et al., 2005) of mice with AraC, a cell proliferation inhibitor, reduced SNI-induced mechanical pain hypersensitivity (mechanical allodynia) that was associated with decreased numbers of CX3CR1+ cells in the DRGs (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The dose of AraC injected intrathecally does not change the baseline of the mechanical nociceptive threshold.
source: Noteworthy, this dose of AraC injected intrathecally did not change the baseline of the mechanical nociceptive threshold (Gu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The CX3CR1+ resident macrophage population is expanding, accounting for the increase in the number of macrophages in the sensory ganglia and neuropathic pain (e.g. mechanical allodynia) development observed after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the CX3CR1+ resident macrophage population is expanding, accounting for the increase in the number of macrophages in the sensory ganglia and neuropathic pain (e.g. mechanical allodynia) development observed after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from proliferation data and AraC treatment effects on pain behavior.

claim: CX3CR1 is expressed in sNAMs.
source: After characterizing the resident macrophages proliferation in the sensory ganglia triggered by peripheral nerve injury, we sought to investigate possible mechanisms involved in this process, since CX3CR1 is expressed in sNAMs (Wang et al., 2020; Kolter et al., 2019; Chakarov et al., 2019) and there is evidence that CX3CR1 signaling mediates microglia proliferation in the spinal cord after peripheral nerve injury (Gu et al., 2016; Suter et al., 2009; Rotterman and Alvarez, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CX3CR1 signaling mediates microglia proliferation in the spinal cord after peripheral nerve injury.
source: After characterizing the resident macrophages proliferation in the sensory ganglia triggered by peripheral nerve injury, we sought to investigate possible mechanisms involved in this process, since CX3CR1 is expressed in sNAMs (Wang et al., 2020; Kolter et al., 2019; Chakarov et al., 2019) and there is evidence that CX3CR1 signaling mediates microglia proliferation in the spinal cord after peripheral nerve injury (Gu et al., 2016; Suter et al., 2009; Rotterman and Alvarez, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The expression of Cx3cl1 increases in the DRGs after SNI.
source: Herein, we also observed that the expression of Cx3cl1, the CX3CR1 ligand, increased in the DRGs after SNI (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice in naive condition do not show any difference in the number of CX3CR1+CD11b+ cells in the sensory ganglia (DRGs L3-L5) compared to heterozygous littermate controls (Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice).
source: Notably, Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice in naive condition did not show any difference in the number of CX3CR1+CD11b+ cells in the sensory ganglia (DRGs L3-L5) compared to heterozygous littermate controls (Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The increase of the CX3CR1+CD11b+ cells population observed after SNI in the DRGs is reduced in the absence of the CX3CR1 signaling.
source: Nevertheless, the increase of the CX3CR1+CD11b+ cells population observed after SNI in the DRGs was reduced in the absence of the CX3CR1 signaling (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data comparing Cx3cr1GFP/GFP and Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There is no difference in the number of CX3CR1+ Iba1+ macrophages in the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice compared to DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice at naive condition.
source: These flow cytometry data were confirmed by immunofluorescence analysis that showed no difference, at the naive condition in the number of CX3CR1+ Iba1+ macrophages in the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice compared to DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The number of CX3CR1+ Iba1+ macrophages after SNI in the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice is reduced when compared to the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice.
source: Furthermore, the number of CX3CR1+ Iba1+ macrophages after SNI in the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice was reduced when compared to the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The number of macrophages proliferating (CX3CR1+ Ki67+ cells) after SNI in the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice is reduced when compared to the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice.
source: Supporting the involvement of CX3CR1 signaling on sNAMs proliferation in the DRGs, we found that the number of macrophages proliferating (CX3CR1+ Ki67+ cells) after SNI in the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice was reduced when compared to the DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: SNI-mechanical pain hypersensitivity is reduced in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice compared to Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice.
source: Finally, we also found that SNI-mechanical pain hypersensitivity was also reduced in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice compared to Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing shown in Figure 7E.

claim: CX3CR1 signaling does not control the survival/seeding of sNAMs in the sensory ganglia.
source: These results suggest that CX3CR1 signaling does not control the survival/seeding of sNAMs in the sensory ganglia, but might be important for their proliferation and consequently to neuropathic pain development after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that baseline macrophage numbers are similar in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP and Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice.

claim: CX3CR1 signaling is important for sNAMs proliferation after peripheral nerve injury.
source: These results suggest that CX3CR1 signaling does not control the survival/seeding of sNAMs in the sensory ganglia, but might be important for their proliferation and consequently to neuropathic pain development after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from reduced proliferation in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice after SNI.

claim: CX3CR1 signaling is important for neuropathic pain development after peripheral nerve injury.
source: These results suggest that CX3CR1 signaling does not control the survival/seeding of sNAMs in the sensory ganglia, but might be important for their proliferation and consequently to neuropathic pain development after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from reduced pain hypersensitivity in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice after SNI.

claim: TNF, IL-1b, and IL-6 are the most important cytokines in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
source: After peripheral nerve injury, the expression of several cytokines and chemokines increases in the sensory ganglia. Among these cytokines, TNF, IL-1b, and IL-6 seem to be the most important (Yu et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is an up-regulation of Tnf, Il1b, and Il6 transcripts in the DRGs of mice 7 days after SNI compared to naive-control mice.
source: Herein, we confirmed this evidence and observed an up-regulation of Tnf, Il1b, and Il6 transcripts in the DRGs of mice 7 days after SNI compared to naive-control mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The expression of Tnf and Il1b after peripheral nerve injury is confined in the sNAMs cluster.
source: In addition, the expression of Tnf and Il1b after peripheral nerve injury was confined in the sNAMs cluster (Figure 8B), while Il6 expression was not conclusively defined (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by re-analysis of single-cell RNAseq data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Il6 expression after peripheral nerve injury is not conclusively defined to a specific cell type in single-cell RNAseq analysis.
source: In addition, the expression of Tnf and Il1b after peripheral nerve injury was confined in the sNAMs cluster (Figure 8B), while Il6 expression was not conclusively defined (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by re-analysis of single-cell RNAseq data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Tnf and Il1b transcripts are detected substantially in CX3CR1+CD11b+ cells harvested from DRGs.
source: We found that Tnf and Il1b transcripts are detected substantially in CX3CR1+CD11b+ cells harvested from DRGs, and their expression increased only in this specific cell population after SNI (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of sorted cells shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tnf and Il1b expression increases only in CX3CR1+CD11b+ cells after SNI.
source: We found that Tnf and Il1b transcripts are detected substantially in CX3CR1+CD11b+ cells harvested from DRGs, and their expression increased only in this specific cell population after SNI (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of sorted cells shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Il6 expression is detected mainly on CD45− cells in the DRGs.
source: On the other hand, Il6 expression was detected mainly on CD45− cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of sorted cells shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tnf and Il1b are reduced in DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice after SNI compared to WT mice.
source: While we detected an increase of Tnf and Il1b in the DRGs from WT mice after SNI, these genes were reduced in DRGs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing Cx3cr1GFP/GFP and WT mice shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Il6 expression increases in the DRGs similarly in both Cx3cr1GFP/GFP and WT mice after SNI.
source: On the other hand, Il6 expression increased in the DRGs similarly in both mice genotypes (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing Cx3cr1GFP/GFP and WT mice shown in Figure 8D.

claim: sNAMs are the main source of CX3CR1 signaling-dependent pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-b and TNF) in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Altogether, these results indicated that sNAMs are the main source of CX3CR1 signaling-dependent pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-b and TNF) in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury, whereas IL-6 seems to be induced mainly in non-immune cells.
evidence: Inferred from cell sorting and CX3CR1 deficiency experiments.

claim: IL-6 is induced mainly in non-immune cells in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Altogether, these results indicated that sNAMs are the main source of CX3CR1 signaling-dependent pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-b and TNF) in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury, whereas IL-6 seems to be induced mainly in non-immune cells.
evidence: Inferred from cell sorting data showing Il6 expression in CD45− cells.

claim: Resident macrophages are distributed across all tissues and are highly heterogeneous due to adaptation to different tissue-specific environments.
source: Resident macrophages are distributed across all tissues and are highly heterogeneous due to adaptation to different tissue-specific environments.
evidence: Represents established scientific knowledge about tissue-resident macrophages.

claim: The resident macrophages of the sensory ganglia (sensory neuron-associated macrophages, sNAMs) are in close contact with the cell body of primary sensory neurons.
source: The resident macrophages of the sensory ganglia (sensory neuron-associated macrophages, sNAMs) are in close contact with the cell body of primary sensory neurons and might play physiological and pathophysiological roles.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about sNAMs location and potential roles.

claim: After peripheral nerve injury, there is an increase in the population of macrophages in the sensory ganglia.
source: After peripheral nerve injury, there is an increase in the population of macrophages in the sensory ganglia, which have been implicated in different conditions, including neuropathic pain development.
evidence: Represents established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Macrophages in the sensory ganglia have been implicated in neuropathic pain development.
source: After peripheral nerve injury, there is an increase in the population of macrophages in the sensory ganglia, which have been implicated in different conditions, including neuropathic pain development.
evidence: Represents established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: It is under debate whether macrophage accumulation in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury is due to the local proliferation of resident macrophages or a result of blood monocyte infiltration.
source: However, it is still under debate whether macrophage accumulation in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury is due to the local proliferation of resident macrophages or a result of blood monocyte infiltration.
evidence: Represents the scientific controversy that this study addresses.

claim: The increase in the number of macrophages in the sensory ganglia after SNI is a consequence of the proliferation of resident CX3CR1+ macrophages.
source: Here, we confirmed that the number of macrophages increased in the sensory ganglia after the spared nerve injury (SNI) model in mice. Using different approaches, we found that the increase in the number of macrophages in the sensory ganglia after SNI is a consequence of the proliferation of resident CX3CR1+ macrophages, which participate in the development of neuropathic pain, but not due to infiltration of peripheral blood monocytes.
evidence: Represents the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: The increase in the number of macrophages in the sensory ganglia after SNI is not due to infiltration of peripheral blood monocytes.
source: Here, we confirmed that the number of macrophages increased in the sensory ganglia after the spared nerve injury (SNI) model in mice. Using different approaches, we found that the increase in the number of macrophages in the sensory ganglia after SNI is a consequence of the proliferation of resident CX3CR1+ macrophages, which participate in the development of neuropathic pain, but not due to infiltration of peripheral blood monocytes.
evidence: Represents the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Proliferating CX3CR1+ macrophages participate in the development of neuropathic pain.
source: Here, we confirmed that the number of macrophages increased in the sensory ganglia after the spared nerve injury (SNI) model in mice. Using different approaches, we found that the increase in the number of macrophages in the sensory ganglia after SNI is a consequence of the proliferation of resident CX3CR1+ macrophages, which participate in the development of neuropathic pain, but not due to infiltration of peripheral blood monocytes.
evidence: Inferred from proliferation inhibition and CX3CR1 deficiency experiments showing reduced pain.

claim: Proliferating macrophages are the source of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL-1b in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
source: These proliferating macrophages are the source of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL-1b.
evidence: Supported by cell sorting and gene expression analysis.

claim: CX3CR1 signaling is involved in the sNAMs proliferation after peripheral nerve injury.
source: In addition, we found that CX3CR1 signaling is involved in the sNAMs proliferation and neuropathic pain development after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Supported by experiments in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice showing reduced proliferation.

claim: CX3CR1 signaling is involved in neuropathic pain development after peripheral nerve injury.
source: In addition, we found that CX3CR1 signaling is involved in the sNAMs proliferation and neuropathic pain development after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Supported by experiments in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice showing reduced pain hypersensitivity.

claim: Peripheral nerve injury leads to sNAMs proliferation in the sensory ganglia in a CX3CR1-dependent manner accounting for neuropathic pain development.
source: In summary, these results indicated that peripheral nerve injury leads to sNAMs proliferation in the sensory ganglia in a CX3CR1-dependent manner accounting for neuropathic pain development.
evidence: Represents the main conclusion of the study, integrating multiple findings.

claim: sNAMs proliferation could be modulated to change pathophysiological conditions such as chronic neuropathic pain.
source: In conclusion, sNAMs proliferation could be modulated to change pathophysiological conditions such as chronic neuropathic pain.
evidence: Represents a speculative therapeutic implication based on the study findings.

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages are well-known for participating in host defense and in the clearance of dead cells and tissue debris.
source: Historically, these resident cells are well-known for participating in host defense and in the clearance of dead cells and tissue debris, contributing to a range of pathological processes (Ginhoux and Guilliams, 2016; Davies et al., 2013; Wynn and Vannella, 2016).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Macrophages are a heterogeneous population, exhibiting high functional plasticity that is correlated with the specific functions of each tissue and niche in which they reside.
source: It has been appreciated that beyond their classical role in inflamed tissues, macrophages are a heterogeneous population, exhibiting high functional plasticity that is correlated with the specific functions of each tissue and niche in which they reside (Epelman et al., 2014; Van Hove et al., 2019).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Macrophages distributed along the sciatic nerve and in the sensory ganglia are in close contact with the primary sensory neurons.
source: In the PNS, macrophages distributed along the sciatic nerve and in the sensory ganglia (e.g. dorsal root ganglia - DRG and trigeminal ganglion) are in close contact with the primary sensory neurons, known as (sNAMs Silva et al., 2021; Kolter et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Resident macrophages in the PNS play a crucial role in nervous tissue repair.
source: These resident macrophages play a crucial role in nervous tissue repair (Feng et al., 2023) and, more recently, they have been described as an important component in the development of neuropathic pain caused by peripheral nerve injury either in male and female mice (Guimarães et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Resident macrophages in the PNS have been described as an important component in the development of neuropathic pain caused by peripheral nerve injury in both male and female mice.
source: These resident macrophages play a crucial role in nervous tissue repair (Feng et al., 2023) and, more recently, they have been described as an important component in the development of neuropathic pain caused by peripheral nerve injury either in male and female mice (Guimarães et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the injured peripheral nerves, the sNAMs functions are associated with phagocytosis of cell debris and release of early inflammatory mediators.
source: In the injured peripheral nerves, the sNAMs functions are associated with phagocytosis of cell debris and release of early inflammatory mediators, which in turn contribute to the recruitment of neutrophils and CCR2-expressing monocytes (Calvo et al., 2012; Kim and Moalem-Taylor, 2011a; Lindborg et al., 2017; Jung et al., 2009).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: sNAMs contribute to the recruitment of neutrophils and CCR2-expressing monocytes in injured peripheral nerves.
source: In the injured peripheral nerves, the sNAMs functions are associated with phagocytosis of cell debris and release of early inflammatory mediators, which in turn contribute to the recruitment of neutrophils and CCR2-expressing monocytes (Calvo et al., 2012; Kim and Moalem-Taylor, 2011a; Lindborg et al., 2017; Jung et al., 2009).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neuroinflammatory response at the level of sensory ganglia is characterized by activation of glial cells and sNAMs and the consequent release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, in particular, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF.
source: These changes propagate the neuroinflammatory response at the level of sensory ganglia characterized by activation of glial cells and sNAMs and the consequent release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, in particular, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF (Yu et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2014).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several studies using different peripheral nerve injury models have described an increase in the number of macrophages/monocytes surrounding the cell body of sensory neurons in the DRGs.
source: Several studies using different peripheral nerve injury models have described an increase in the number of macrophages/monocytes surrounding the cell body of sensory neurons in the DRGs (Kwon et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2011b; Huang et al., 2014; Kallenborn-Gerhardt et al., 2014; Luo et al., 2019; Kalinski et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have referred to the increase in macrophages in the DRGs as a result of the infiltration of peripheral blood monocytes.
source: Although these studies have referred to this increase as a result of the infiltration of peripheral blood monocytes, recent studies have suggested that resident sNAMs, in the DRGs, also proliferate after peripheral nerve injury (Iwai et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents previous interpretation in the literature.

claim: Recent studies have suggested that resident sNAMs in the DRGs proliferate after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Although these studies have referred to this increase as a result of the infiltration of peripheral blood monocytes, recent studies have suggested that resident sNAMs, in the DRGs, also proliferate after peripheral nerve injury (Iwai et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents recent findings in the literature supported by citations.

claim: The blood dorsal root ganglion barrier is formed by the perineurium and endoneurial blood vessels.
source: Although the reasons are not immediately apparent, the possible explanation is the blood dorsal root ganglion barrier, formed by the perineurium and endoneurial blood vessels. This barrier protects and maintains the PNS in an appropriate physicochemical environment (Reinhold and Rittner, 2020).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The blood dorsal root ganglion barrier protects and maintains the PNS in an appropriate physicochemical environment.
source: Although the reasons are not immediately apparent, the possible explanation is the blood dorsal root ganglion barrier, formed by the perineurium and endoneurial blood vessels. This barrier protects and maintains the PNS in an appropriate physicochemical environment (Reinhold and Rittner, 2020).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The perineurium is a thick layer of connective tissue whose cells have a non-polarized architecture and are interconnected by tight junctions, gap junctions, and adherens junctions.
source: The perineurium is a thick layer of connective tissue whose cells have a non-polarized architecture and are interconnected by tight junctions (TJ), gap junctions, and adherens junctions (AJ), similar to the composition of the CNS blood-brain barrier.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about perineurium structure.

claim: The endoneurial vessels are composed of a network of arterioles, venules, and non-fenestrated capillaries.
source: The endoneurial vessels are composed of a network of arterioles, venules, and non-fenestrated capillaries. The endothelial cells that create this vascular network are also sealed by TJ, but more permeable than the perineurium, since there must be a controlled exchange between blood and nerve to allow neural nutrition (Reinhold and Rittner, 2017).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The endothelial cells of endoneurial vessels are sealed by tight junctions but are more permeable than the perineurium.
source: The endoneurial vessels are composed of a network of arterioles, venules, and non-fenestrated capillaries. The endothelial cells that create this vascular network are also sealed by TJ, but more permeable than the perineurium, since there must be a controlled exchange between blood and nerve to allow neural nutrition (Reinhold and Rittner, 2017).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: After crush injury, there may be a loss and recovery of the blood dorsal root ganglion barrier junction, associated with the expression of intercellular junctional proteins.
source: Previous studies suggest that after crush injury, there may be a loss and recovery of the blood dorsal root ganglion barrier junction, associated with the expression of intercellular junctional proteins (Hirakawa et al., 2003).
evidence: Represents previous findings supported by citation.

claim: CD8+ T cells do not infiltrate the sensory ganglia of adult mice after peripheral nerve injury.
source: A recent study shows that CD8+ T cells, that did not infiltrate the sensory ganglia of adult mice after peripheral nerve injury, are able to infiltrate when the injury is performed in 2 years old mice (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: Represents recent findings supported by citation.

claim: CD8+ T cells are able to infiltrate the sensory ganglia when peripheral nerve injury is performed in 2 years old mice.
source: A recent study shows that CD8+ T cells, that did not infiltrate the sensory ganglia of adult mice after peripheral nerve injury, are able to infiltrate when the injury is performed in 2 years old mice (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: Represents recent findings supported by citation.

claim: The process of aging might alter the sensory ganglia-blood barrier.
source: These data indicate that the process of aging might alter the sensory ganglia-blood barrier.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that aged mice show different infiltration patterns.

claim: There is recent evidence of accumulation of leukocytes into the dorsal root leptomeninges that cover the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
source: In addition, although immune cells seem to be unable to infiltrate the cell-body-rich area of the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury (at least in young mice), there is recent evidence of accumulation of leukocytes into the dorsal root leptomeninges that cover the sensory ganglia (Du et al., 2018; Maganin et al., 2022).
evidence: Represents recent findings supported by citations.

claim: Constant activation of neurons following peripheral nerve injury results in CX3CL1 production in the spinal cord.
source: Some studies have indicated that constant activation of neurons following peripheral nerve injury results in CX3CL1 production in the spinal cord, which in turn induces activation/proliferation of local microglia (Verge et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2016; Clark et al., 2007).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CX3CL1 production in the spinal cord induces activation/proliferation of local microglia.
source: Some studies have indicated that constant activation of neurons following peripheral nerve injury results in CX3CL1 production in the spinal cord, which in turn induces activation/proliferation of local microglia (Verge et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2016; Clark et al., 2007).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the DRG, the CX3CR1-proliferating macrophages are in close contact with the cell body of sensory neurons, which constitutively express the membrane-bound CX3CL1.
source: In fact, in the DRG, the CX3CR1-proliferating macrophages are in close contact with the cell body of sensory neurons, which constitutively express the membrane-bound CX3CL1 (Kim et al., 2011c; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: Represents established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: After peripheral nerve injury, membrane-bound CX3CL1 is reduced in the cell bodies of sensory neurons, suggesting their release and action in the sNAMs.
source: Moreover, after peripheral nerve injury, membrane-bound CX3CL1 is reduced in the cell bodies of sensory neurons, suggesting their release and action in the sNAMs (Zhuang et al., 2007).
evidence: Represents previous findings supported by citation and inference about mechanism.

claim: Other signaling pathways besides CX3CR1 are involved in the activation/proliferation of sNAMs in the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Since the increase in the number of sNAMs was only partially reduced in CX3CR1 deficient mice, it is plausible that other signaling pathways are involved in the activation/proliferation of sNAMs in the DRGs after peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from the partial reduction in macrophage expansion in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice.

claim: CSF1-CSF1R signaling is involved in sNAMs expansion in sensory ganglia.
source: One possibility that has been recently explored is the CSF1-CSF1R signaling. In fact, injured neurons produce and release CSF-1 that in turn promotes sNAMs expansion in sensory ganglia through CSF1R activation (Guan et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents recent findings supported by citations.

claim: Injured neurons produce and release CSF-1 that promotes sNAMs expansion in sensory ganglia through CSF1R activation.
source: One possibility that has been recently explored is the CSF1-CSF1R signaling. In fact, injured neurons produce and release CSF-1 that in turn promotes sNAMs expansion in sensory ganglia through CSF1R activation (Guan et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents recent findings supported by citations.

claim: sNAMs in the sensory ganglia express Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and nucleotide-binding cytoplasmic oligomerization (Nod)-like receptors (NLRs).
source: Like classic cells in the innate immune system, sNAMs in the sensory ganglia also express Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and nucleotide-binding cytoplasmic oligomerization (Nod)-like receptors (NLRs).
evidence: Represents established knowledge about sNAMs.

claim: Activation of sNAMs in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury depends on downstream signaling generated by the activation of TLR2, TLR4, and TLR9.
source: Previous studies indicate that activation of sNAMs in the sensory ganglia, after peripheral nerve injury, depends on downstream signaling generated by the activation of TLR2, TLR4, and TLR9 (Shen et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2011b; Luo et al., 2019).
evidence: Represents previous findings supported by citations.

claim: NOD2 deficiency prevents the increase in the number of sNAMs in the DRGs after SNI.
source: We also demonstrated that NOD2 deficiency prevented the increase in the number of sNAMs in the DRGs after SNI (Guimarães et al., 2019).
evidence: Represents previous findings from the authors' group supported by citation.

claim: There are discrepancies in the literature regarding the cellular source of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the sensory ganglia after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Although there is a consensus that peripheral nerve injury triggers the up-regulation of these cytokines in the sensory ganglia, their cellular source is not completely characterized and there are discrepancies in the literature.
evidence: Represents the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The production of TNF and IL-1b by sNAMs in the sensory ganglia has been implicated in the pathophysiology of neuropathic pain.
source: The production of these cytokines by sNAMs in the sensory ganglia has been recently implicated in the pathophysiology of neuropathic pain (Guimarães et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents recent findings supported by citations.

claim: Sensory neurons produce IL-6 after different nerve injuries.
source: These data are consistent with previous reports indicating that sensory neurons start to produce IL-6 after different nerve injuries (Murphy et al., 1995; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: Represents previous findings supported by citations.

claim: CX3CR1 signaling is not involved in IL-6 production after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Furthermore, our data show that CX3CR1 signaling is not involved in the IL-6 production after peripheral nerve injury, further support the independence of its production by sNAMs.
evidence: Supported by data showing similar IL-6 expression in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP and WT mice.
